subject: Business
title: How Credit Scores Work
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on How Credit Scores Work.

hook.text: A three-digit number determines if you get a mortgage, what interest rate you pay, and sometimes if you get hired.

buildup.text: A credit score (300-850) represents your creditworthiness based on your borrowing and repayment history.

discovery.text: Five factors: payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), length of history (15%), new credit (10%), credit mix (10%).

twist.text: Closing old credit cards hurts your score by reducing available credit and shortening your history.

climax.text: A 100-point difference can mean $50,000 more in mortgage interest over 30 years. The score has real cost.

punchline.text: Your credit score is your financial reputation in a single number.

quiz.question: What is the largest factor in a credit score?

details.summary: Credit scores are three-digit numbers ranging from 300 to 850 that predict your likelihood of repaying debt. Payment history and credit utilization make up the largest factors, determining the interest rates and credit limits lenders will offer you.
details.whyItMatters: Your credit score affects mortgage rates, credit card terms, rental approvals, and even job eligibility. A higher score can save tens of thousands of dollars over a lifetime through lower interest rates on major purchases.
takeaways: Payment history is the single largest factor at 35 percent of your score
Keep credit utilization below 30 percent of available credit limits
A higher score means lower interest rates and better financial opportunities

faq.question: What are the five factors that determine a FICO credit score?
faq.answer: Payment history at 35 percent, amounts owed relative to limits at 30 percent, length of credit history at 15 percent, credit mix at 10 percent, and new credit inquiries at 10 percent. Paying on time and keeping balances low together drive nearly two-thirds of the score.

faq.question: How quickly can you improve a bad credit score?
faq.answer: Positive changes in utilization reflect within 30 to 60 days. Late payments stay on reports for seven years but their impact fades over time. Consistent on-time payments and reducing balances can raise a score by 100 points or more within six to twelve months.
